newsitem.title: UK: UK doctors reject call for legal mercy killings.
newsitem.headline: UK doctors reject call for legal mercy killings.

text.p: British doctors on Thursday voted forcefully against any change in the law that bars doctors from carrying out mercy killings or helping dying patients to kill themselves.
The doctors gathered in Edinburgh for the annual conference of the British Medical Association (BMA) passed the motion after a lengthy and sometimes emotional debate.

The vote was a robust response to calls from some doctors for changes in the law. Only about 20 doctors voted against the motion for the law to be left unchanged and none spoke in favour of legalising mercy killings.
Sandy Macara, chairman of the BMA council made clear his association's position.
"Others rightly see us saving life, not embracing death. We should not do anything to betray that trust in our essential vital function." Macara said.
Several doctors described the agonising decisions they had faced when terminally ill patients had appealed to them for help to end their suffering.
One told how he had refused to help one patient to end his life, only for the patient to go home and shoot himself in the head a few days later.
"I've been faced by patients requesting assistance in ending their lives and I've received their thanks in not having done so," another doctor, Fay Wilson told the conference.
"We must not change the rules which will put us on a slippery slope to expectation that our function is to put out of the way and kill people who we see as not worthwhile," Wilson said.

Assisted suicide had a paternalistic tinge, said Dr Stuart Horner of the BMA's ethics committee. "The doctor decides whether the patient's condition would justify death...the doctor decides the most appropriate form of termination.
"The fact that the patient completes the task hardly makes the whole process autonomous."
Despite the BMA's solidarity on Thursday's vote, there have been growing calls in Britain for the legalisation of euthanasia and assisted suicide.

The issue has been highlighted by the case of motor neurone disease sufferer Annie Lindsell who has asked the High Court to allow her doctor to give her drugs likely to shorten her life once she becomes incapacitated by the disease.
The doctors made no reference to her case in Thursday's debate, but one speaker approved of the U.S. Supreme Court's decision last month to keep doctor-assisted suicides outside the law.
The BMA vote contrasted with a survey of 1,000 doctors and pharmacists last year that found 51 percent would be willing to help a patient to commit suicide if the law allowed them to do so.
Some doctors have admitted helping patients in this way, despite the fact that assisting a suicide can carry a jail sentence of up to 14 years in England and Wales, though not in Scotland.
